title: In-Context / Few-Shot Learning
oneLineScope: GPT-3 and few-shot prompting: how to specify a task purely in the prompt — no weight updates, no gradient steps — and have a large frozen model perform it.
prose:
Where we are. The scaling laws node established that language model performance follows orderly power laws across compute, data, and parameters — and that some capabilities do not appear at all until models cross certain size thresholds. That observation left a question open: what, exactly, becomes possible at scale that was not possible before? One concrete answer turned up in 2020. GPT-3, at 175 billion parameters, could perform a task it had never been explicitly trained on, simply by reading a description of the task — optionally with a handful of examples — in the input text. No weight updates. No gradient steps. No new training run.

The gist. In-context learning is the ability to specify a task entirely within the prompt — as a natural-language instruction, with zero, one, or a few worked examples — and have a large frozen model perform it. The parameters \(\theta\) do not change; whatever conditioning on the examples occurs happens inside the forward pass, as the transformer’s attention layers process the full prompt. The word “learning” here is deliberately loose: no state is written, no gradient is computed. A better gloss might be in-context conditioning — the model’s output distribution is steered by what it reads. The capability is real, measurable, and — this is the key finding — a property of scale: small models show negligible benefit from in-context examples; large models exploit them aggressively.

Why it matters. Before GPT-3, deploying a model on a new task meant a new fine-tuning run: labeled data, gradient updates, a separate checkpoint per task. In-context learning collapses that overhead to writing a prompt. It also changed what a language model is conceptually — not a narrow classifier to be fine-tuned for each application, but a general-purpose conditional distribution steerable by natural language. The field’s trajectory from 2020 onward — prompt engineering, instruction tuning, RLHF — follows directly from taking that observation seriously. It is also the direct empirical consequence of the scaling curve: the capability was not engineered in; it emerged.

Prompting as task specification

The idea is clearest at its extremes. In zero-shot prompting, the input is a plain instruction — “Translate English to French: ‘the cat sat on the mat’ →” — with no worked examples. The model must infer everything about the task from the description alone. In one-shot prompting, a single input–output demonstration precedes the query, giving the model a concrete instance of the expected format. In few-shot prompting, \(K\) such demonstrations appear — typically \(K \in \{8, 16, 32\}\), bounded by the context window — before the item the model must complete.

A few-shot prompt has a fixed skeleton:

Instruction: [task description in natural language]

Input: [example input 1]  Output: [example output 1]
Input: [example input 2]  Output: [example output 2]
       ... (K times) ...
Input: [query input]       Output:

The model’s completion of that final blank is the prediction. The weights \(\theta\) are frozen throughout. The demonstrations constrain the output distribution: they establish the vocabulary of valid responses (“Positive” or “Negative” rather than any arbitrary token), disambiguate the task, and correct formatting or phrasing biases. The query is answered not because the model was trained to answer it, but because a careful completion of this particular string happens to be the answer — and a sufficiently large model, having seen the shape of this kind of text during pretraining, assigns that completion high probability.

What the “learning” is and is not

Brown et al. raise this question honestly and do not fully answer it — and it is worth pausing on, because the mechanism is not settled. No parameters are updated. The model does not become a sentiment classifier; it generates the most probable continuation of the prompt, and the prompt is structured so that the correct label is a probable next token. The mechanistic account — exactly what the attention layers compute when they exploit in-context examples — is active research, not established science.

A careful ablation by Min et al. (2022) adds a clarifying wrinkle: the labels themselves in the few-shot examples matter less than one might expect. Replacing correct labels with random labels often barely degrades performance. The examples primarily serve to establish the output format and response distribution — not to teach the label–input mapping. The model is not learning from your three demonstrations that “sad movie reviews go to Negative”; it is mostly learning what Negative looks like as a completion in this context. What the examples install is format and vocabulary, not a task-specific inference rule. Keep this in mind when interpreting benchmark numbers: they are numbers under a particular prompt, not fixed capability scores.

GPT-3 at 175 billion parameters

GPT-3 is an autoregressive decoder-only transformer — the architecture covered in the autoregressive language modeling node — trained on roughly 300 billion tokens drawn from filtered CommonCrawl, WebText2, Books1, Books2, and English Wikipedia. Its 175 billion parameters made it the largest language model publicly reported at the time. The key hyperparameters: \(d_{\text{model}} = 12{,}288\), \(h = 96\) attention heads, \(L = 96\) layers, context window of 2,048 tokens. Training used the standard causal language-model objective

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{t} \log P_{\theta}(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}) \]

where \(\theta\) are the parameters, \(x_1, \ldots, x_T\) are the tokens of a document, and the sum runs over positions \(t\). There is nothing novel in the training procedure; the novelty is scale, and what emerged from it.

What GPT-3 could do in context

Brown et al. evaluated GPT-3 across a wide range of tasks — translation, question answering, reading comprehension, arithmetic, commonsense reasoning, Winograd schemas — using only prompt engineering, without any gradient steps. A few results worth anchoring to:

  • On SuperGLUE, GPT-3 few-shot approached fine-tuned BERT-large on several subtasks without touching the model’s weights. On others it fell short; the results were uneven, not uniformly triumphant.
  • On translation from English to French, German, and Romanian, few-shot GPT-3 was competitive with supervised models trained on those specific language pairs.
  • On arithmetic (three-digit addition, subtraction, multiplication), few-shot performance was surprisingly strong, though it degraded as the number of digits grew.

The paper’s §3.3 establishes the scaling relationship directly: zero-shot performance improves modestly from 1B to 175B parameters, but the gap between zero-shot and few-shot widens sharply as the model grows. Small models at 1B parameters show negligible benefit from in-context examples; the GPT-3-scale model exploits them aggressively. This is the direct empirical link back to scaling laws: in-context ability is not a fixed property of the architecture; it is something that emerges — and strengthens — with scale.

Prompt sensitivity and other honest caveats

Brown et al. are candid about several problems. Prompt sensitivity is the most practically important: the order of the few-shot examples, the exact phrasing of the instruction, and even the formatting of separators can shift performance by more than ten percentage points on a task. Reported benchmark numbers therefore depend on prompt-design choices that are hard to justify systematically. Calibration is a second problem: GPT-3 is often confidently wrong, and its probability estimates do not reliably track correctness. The model also repeats itself and can degenerate on long outputs. These are acknowledged in the paper, not retrofitted apologies.

The deeper conceptual constraint is structural: because no gradient steps occur, in-context learning can only steer toward behaviors the pretraining distribution already made probable. If a mapping is genuinely foreign to the pretraining corpus, a handful of in-context examples will not install it. The model is a heavily pretrained distribution that conditions on context, not a blank slate that learns from demonstration. Working within that constraint is what prompt engineering is.

The contrast with fine-tuning

Fine-tuning in the GPT-1 / BERT sense updates \(\theta\): you continue training on task-specific data with a cross-entropy loss, the weights shift to encode task structure, and the model’s behavior on that checkpoint is permanently altered. Fine-tuning tends to outperform few-shot prompting on individual tasks where sufficient labeled data exist — particularly for structured-output tasks where the desired behavior is precise. But it requires labeled data, a training run, and a separate checkpoint per task: costs that scale poorly when the number of tasks is large or the compute budget is limited. In-context learning amortizes those costs to a prompt written at inference time. Neither approach strictly dominates; the tradeoff depends on data availability, task count, and latency constraints.

This contrast is the setup for the next node. Supervised fine-tuning is not a retreat from the in-context paradigm — it is an attempt to make the base model a more reliable instruction follower by training it on instruction–response demonstrations, so that prompting becomes less fragile without paying the per-task fine-tuning cost in perpetuity.

Where it leads

In-context learning reframed what a pretrained language model is: not a narrow text predictor requiring task-specific surgery, but a general-purpose conditional distribution steerable by natural language. The immediate follow-on question is whether we can make that steering more reliable by training the model to be a deliberate instruction follower — which is what supervised fine-tuning addresses. That is the final node in this tutorial, and it closes the arc from raw pretraining to the instruction-following models that became the basis of the first generation of deployed conversational assistants.

diagrams.caption: Few-shot prompting feeds a frozen model an instruction, K input–output example pairs, then a query; the model completes the final output without any weight update. Contrasted with fine-tuning, where the model's weights are updated by gradient descent on labeled task data.
diagrams.altText: Left panel labeled 'In-context / few-shot learning': a prompt box containing an instruction row, three input–output example rows, and a query row feeds via an arrow into a frozen model box (labeled 'model (frozen)', with 'weights θ unchanged' noted beneath). An arrow exits to a completion box. Right panel labeled 'Fine-tuning (for contrast)': a task dataset box containing instruction–response pairs feeds via a gradient-update arrow into a base model box, which leads to a fine-tuned model box labeled θ′ with 'weights θ modified' noted. The two panels are separated by a vertical dashed line with 'vs.' in the middle.
diagrams.prompt: Structural comparison diagram split left and right by a vertical dashed divider labeled 'vs.' in the middle. Left side, titled 'In-context / few-shot learning': a tall vertically-oriented prompt box (outlined in blue) containing, from top to bottom: a row labeled 'instruction', then three rows each with an 'input N' box and an 'output N' box connected by a right-arrow (the output boxes in green), a small annotation 'K = 3 examples', and finally a row with a 'query' box (blue) pointing to a dashed empty '?' box. An arrow leads rightward from the prompt box into a 'model (frozen)' box; annotate the model with 'weights θ unchanged'. An arrow exits the model to a small 'completion' box (green). Right side, titled 'Fine-tuning (for contrast)': a 'Task dataset' box containing two instruction→response pair rows feeds downward via an arrow labeled 'gradient update (∂𝓛/∂θ)' into a 'base model + training step' box (outlined in red); an arrow exits right to a 'fine-tuned model (θ′)' box (green, stroke-width thicker), annotated 'weights θ modified'. Bottom annotations: left side 'Forward pass only — no weight changes'; right side 'Weights updated by cross-entropy loss'. Label every element; K = 3 shown explicitly.

diagrams.caption: Accuracy on a representative task rises with the number of in-context examples, and the benefit scales sharply with model size. Small models show negligible gain; large models (GPT-3 scale) show steep improvement. The zero-shot baseline is marked at K = 0.
diagrams.altText: A schematic line chart. Horizontal axis: number of in-context examples K, from 0 (zero-shot) through 1 (one-shot) to few (3–5) and many (10+). Vertical axis: task accuracy. Three curves: a nearly flat grey curve labeled 'small model (little benefit)', a moderately rising blue curve labeled 'medium model', and a steeply rising green curve labeled 'large model (e.g. GPT-3 175B)'. A vertical dashed line at K = 0 is labeled 'zero-shot'. An annotation box reads: 'Few-shot gap widens with scale — a pattern that emerged sharply around 100B+ parameters (Brown et al. 2020, §3.3; emergent is debated — see prose)'.
diagrams.prompt: Conceptual schematic line chart showing how in-context accuracy varies with the number of examples (K) and with model scale. Horizontal axis labeled 'number of in-context examples (K)'; tick marks at 0, 1, 'few (3–5)', and 'many (10+)'. Vertical axis labeled 'task accuracy'. A vertical dashed grey line at K = 0 labeled 'zero-shot'. Three rising curves from left to right: (1) a near-flat muted grey curve labeled 'small model (little benefit)'; (2) a moderately rising blue curve labeled 'medium model'; (3) a steeply rising green curve labeled 'large model (e.g. GPT-3 175B)'. Add a small annotation box inside the chart reading: 'Few-shot gap widens with scale — a pattern that emerged sharply around 100B+ parameters (Brown et al. 2020, §3.3; "emergent" is debated — see prose)'. bibliography.citation: Brown, T., et al. (2020). "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners." NeurIPS 33.
bibliography.annotation: The GPT-3 paper. §1 introduces the zero/one/few-shot taxonomy and the core claim. §3 reports the task evaluations with the scaling breakdown. §3.3 specifically shows the few-shot gap widening with model scale. Appendix G gives the full list of evaluation prompts and is instructive for understanding prompt sensitivity. Read §1 and §3 for the core; §4 for the honest discussion of limitations.

bibliography.citation: Bommasani, R., et al. (2021). "On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models." Stanford CRFM.
bibliography.annotation: A broad survey covering in-context learning in §4.1 with clear conceptual framing. Not a deep technical reference, but situates GPT-3-style prompting in the landscape of what changed in 2020–21. Useful for the reader who wants the wider context before diving into the original paper. Appropriately candid about what is and is not understood mechanistically.

bibliography.citation: Min, S., et al. (2022). "Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations for In-Context Learning." EMNLP.
bibliography.annotation: A careful ablation study showing that the labels in few-shot examples matter less than one might expect — swapping them for random labels often barely degrades performance, suggesting the examples primarily establish format rather than conveying label–input mappings. Important calibrating result for understanding what in-context learning actually does; directly relevant to the 'mechanistic account is open' caveat in the prose. §3–4 are the key sections.
